analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the repeal of the estate tax on very large inheritances.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law had temporarily repealed the federal estate tax, with the tax scheduled to come back in 2011. This bill would have made that repeal permanent, eliminating the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax and keeping the reduced gift tax [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. The estate tax is owed only by estates above a high exemption threshold, so repeal would concentrate its benefits on the wealthiest families. Reduced gift-tax rates would likewise benefit people transferring large fortunes during their lifetimes [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the 2001 law's repeal of the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, which were otherwise set to return in 2011 [S2] [S3].
Permanently keeps the gift-tax reductions from the 2001 law, lowering the cost of large lifetime transfers of wealth [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Eliminating a permanent source of revenue means larger deficits, or higher taxes and smaller services for everyone else to make up the difference.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates a tax that applies only to the very largest estates, so its benefits would flow almost entirely to the wealthiest households while the revenue loss is borne by everyone else through deficits or offsetting cuts [S2] [S3].
Repeal is permanent under the bill, so the revenue loss compounds every year rather than expiring with the 2001 tax law's sunset [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is large but narrow: concentrated on the heirs of multi-million-dollar estates. The cost is spread across all taxpayers through lost federal revenue, which must be replaced by borrowing or by other taxes and cuts. The bill offers no offsetting benefit to ordinary working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Kevin Brady introduced the bill on July 31, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
Thirty-seven members cosponsored the bill: 34 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place; the bill's only recorded actions are its introduction and referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the estate tax remained in place, and the revenue it raises from the largest estates was preserved for the Treasury rather than handed to the heirs of the wealthiest families.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers kept the estate tax

for.name: Kevin Brady
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the estate tax repeal permanent and recruited 37 cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 34 of the bill's 37 cosponsors were House Republicans, with 3 Democrats joining.

industries.note: Full permanent repeal would eliminate a tax owed only by the largest estates, transferring its full value to heirs of the wealthiest families. The lost revenue would be made up by everyone else through deficits or other taxes.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: Permanent repeal would sharply reduce demand for estate-tax planning services built around the tax. Their loss mirrors the public's gain of keeping the tax on large inheritances.
